title: Desmopressin: Replace ADH Without Diluting Sodium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Desmopressin provides antidiuretic effect for central diabetes insipidus and selected bleeding indications, but excess water retention can cause life-threatening hyponatremia. Safe care pairs symptom control with sodium and fluid-balance monitoring rather than treating falling urine output as an automatic success.
recognize: Central diabetes insipidus causes excessive dilute urine and thirst; desmopressin reduces free-water loss.
Headache, nausea, confusion, lethargy, seizure, or unexpected weight gain can signal water intoxication and hyponatremia.
priorities: Verify the indication, baseline sodium, fluid plan, renal function, and interacting medications.
Track urine output, intake, weight, thirst, and neurologic symptoms after administration.
Escalate falling sodium, new confusion, seizure, or unexpected fluid retention immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend serum sodium, fluid balance, weight, urine volume/concentration when ordered, renal function, and neurologic status.
interventions: Follow the prescribed fluid-intake plan; do not encourage unrestricted oral fluids simply because the patient reports thirst.
Use the correct formulation and route because desmopressin products are not automatically interchangeable.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. injection labeling carries a boxed warning for potentially life-threatening hyponatremia.
Loop diuretics, systemic or inhaled glucocorticoids, excessive fluid intake, and illnesses causing fluid/electrolyte imbalance can increase hyponatremia risk or make therapy inappropriate.
redFlags: Marked weight gain with low urine output
teaching: Teach the prescribed fluid limits and the need to report severe headache, confusion, nausea, unusual drowsiness, or sudden weight gain.
delegationScope: Routine intake/output and weight collection may be delegated with clear thresholds; interpretation of sodium or neurologic change requires licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Giving extra free water to a patient on desmopressin because the urine output has fallen and the patient still feels thirsty.
oneLinePearl: Desmopressin saves water—so watch sodium before the brain pays the price.
sourceBasis: DailyMed desmopressin acetate injection U.S. prescribing information, current through 2026

title: Octreotide: Slow Secretions, Watch Glucose and Conduction
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Octreotide suppresses several gastrointestinal and endocrine secretions and may be used for conditions such as acromegaly, carcinoid/VIP syndromes and selected acute bleeding protocols. It can disturb glucose, slow cardiac conduction, and cause biliary complications, so symptom improvement does not eliminate monitoring needs.
recognize: Bradycardia, conduction changes, abdominal pain from biliary disease, and either hypo- or hyperglycemia can occur.
Longer therapy can affect gallbladder, thyroid function, fat absorption, and vitamin B12 status.
priorities: Verify indication, route, glucose status, cardiac history, and interacting rate-slowing medications.
Monitor pulse/rhythm and glucose closely when IV or acute therapy is used.
Escalate symptomatic bradycardia, high-grade block, severe glucose disturbance, or suspected acute biliary complication.
assessMonitor: Trend heart rate/rhythm, glucose, GI symptoms, liver/biliary symptoms, and thyroid/B12 monitoring when long-term therapy is used.
interventions: Administer according to product-specific route and monitoring requirements.
Coordinate diabetes medication changes only through the prescribed plan when glucose shifts occur.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling warns about bradycardia, arrhythmias and higher-degree AV block, especially with IV administration.
Octreotide can cause both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia; never assume it always lowers glucose.
teaching: Teach patients on chronic therapy to report persistent abdominal pain, jaundice, palpitations, fainting, or marked glucose changes.
delegationScope: Routine glucose or pulse collection can be delegated with thresholds; interpretation of rhythm, biliary symptoms, or acute glucose deterioration requires licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Assuming octreotide cannot cause hyperglycemia because it suppresses endocrine secretions.
oneLinePearl: Octreotide quiets secretions—but it can unsettle glucose, rhythm, and the gallbladder.
sourceBasis: DailyMed octreotide acetate injection U.S. prescribing information

title: Albumin Infusion: Expand Plasma, Do Not Flood the Patient
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Human albumin increases intravascular oncotic pressure and can expand plasma volume. The major nursing risk is assuming more volume is always better: patients with heart failure, renal dysfunction, pulmonary edema, anemia or bleeding require careful hemodynamic and fluid reassessment during infusion.
recognize: Albumin can pull fluid into the vascular space and worsen pulmonary congestion or hypertension in susceptible patients.
Hypotension or hypersensitivity can also occur despite its volume-expanding role.
priorities: Assess indication, baseline BP, lungs, edema, oxygenation, urine output, volume status, hemoglobin/hematocrit and cardiac/renal risk.
Monitor during infusion for dyspnea, crackles, rising BP, JVD, hypoxemia, or allergic reaction.
Stop/escalate if cardiovascular overload or serious hypersensitivity develops.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, heart rate, oxygenation, lung sounds, urine output, edema, weight, electrolytes, hematocrit and coagulation context as clinically indicated.
interventions: Use the ordered concentration and infusion rate; do not accelerate simply because BP is low without reassessing the cause.
Maintain access to emergency treatment for hypersensitivity.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling warns about hypervolemia/hemodilution, hypotension, electrolyte imbalance and hypersensitivity.
Albumin should not be diluted with sterile water for injection because hemolysis can occur.
teaching: Explain that breathing difficulty or chest tightness during the infusion should be reported immediately.
delegationScope: Albumin infusion administration and reassessment require facility-defined competency; new cardiopulmonary changes require licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Speeding up albumin in a hypotensive patient who is developing crackles and JVD.
oneLinePearl: Albumin expands the tank—watch the lungs while you fill it.

title: IV Iron Sucrose: Replete Iron, Watch for Reaction
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV iron sucrose treats iron deficiency, commonly in chronic kidney disease, but serious hypersensitivity and clinically significant hypotension can occur. Safe administration means confirming iron need, monitoring during and after the dose, and avoiding repeated iron when stores are already excessive.
recognize: Dizziness, flushing, chest discomfort, wheeze, hypotension, loss of consciousness, or collapse during/after infusion may signal a serious reaction.
Ferritin and transferrin saturation trends help distinguish persistent iron deficiency from iron overload.
priorities: Verify indication, iron studies/hematologic plan, allergy history, BP, and product/dose.
Observe during and after administration with emergency treatment immediately available.
Stop and escalate suspected serious hypersensitivity or clinically significant hypotension.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, symptoms during infusion, hemoglobin response, ferritin/transferrin saturation, and signs of iron overload.
interventions: Administer by the ordered slow IV injection or infusion method and maintain post-dose observation per product/facility requirements.
medicationSafety: Current labeling requires monitoring for hypersensitivity during and after administration and observation for at least 30 minutes until clinically stable.
Do not continue iron simply because anemia persists if iron stores are adequate or excessive; investigate the cause.
teaching: Tell patients to report chest tightness, trouble breathing, dizziness, swelling, or severe weakness during and after treatment.
delegationScope: IV iron administration requires facility-defined competency; assessment of hypersensitivity or hypotension cannot be delegated.
examTrap: Leaving immediately after the infusion finishes because the patient had no reaction during the infusion itself.
oneLinePearl: IV iron can react late—observe after the bag is empty.
sourceBasis: DailyMed iron sucrose injection U.S. prescribing information, current 2026

title: Sevelamer: Bind Phosphate With Meals
bottomLine: Sevelamer binds dietary phosphate in the gut, so timing with meals is part of the drug's mechanism. It does not rapidly correct a dangerous serum phosphorus emergency, and significant GI obstruction or injury risk matters more than simply getting every scheduled dose in.
recognize: Because it works in the GI tract, doses separated from food lose intended phosphate-binding effect.
Severe constipation, dysphagia, abdominal distention, vomiting, GI bleeding, or obstruction symptoms are not routine side effects to ignore.
priorities: Verify phosphorus trend, meal timing, bowel function, swallowing ability, and interacting oral medications.
Administer with meals as prescribed.
Hold/clarify and escalate suspected bowel obstruction or major GI injury.
assessMonitor: Trend serum phosphorus, calcium, bicarbonate as clinically indicated, bowel pattern, swallowing tolerance, and adherence with meal-linked dosing.
interventions: Coordinate administration with meals and product-specific preparation instructions.
Review medication timing because sevelamer may affect absorption of selected oral drugs.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling contraindicates use in bowel obstruction and warns about serious dysphagia, obstruction, ulceration, necrosis and perforation.
Do not crush or alter formulations without verifying product-specific instructions.
teaching: Teach that the medication belongs with meals because it binds the phosphorus in food.
delegationScope: Routine administration can occur within medication scope; new obstruction or swallowing findings require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving sevelamer at bedtime several hours after the patient's last meal because it is listed as a scheduled medication.
oneLinePearl: No meal, little phosphate to bind—timing is part of sevelamer therapy.
sourceBasis: DailyMed sevelamer carbonate U.S. prescribing information, current 2026

title: Cinacalcet: Lower PTH Without Crashing Calcium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Cinacalcet increases calcium-sensing receptor sensitivity and lowers parathyroid hormone, but it can drive calcium dangerously low. Paresthesias, cramps, tetany, seizure, QT prolongation, hypotension or dysrhythmia require prompt recognition rather than being dismissed as dialysis symptoms.
recognize: Hypocalcemia can present with tingling, muscle spasms, tetany, seizure or rhythm change.
The medication is commonly used for secondary hyperparathyroidism in dialysis and selected hypercalcemic parathyroid conditions.
priorities: Verify corrected calcium before initiation/administration according to the plan and review PTH/phosphorus context.
Assess for neuromuscular symptoms and cardiac risk when calcium is falling.
Escalate symptomatic hypocalcemia, seizure, marked QT prolongation or ventricular dysrhythmia.
assessMonitor: Trend corrected calcium, phosphorus, PTH, ECG/QT when clinically indicated, and symptoms of hypocalcemia.
interventions: Administer with food or shortly after a meal per labeling and avoid independent dose changes based on one PTH value.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling contraindicates initiation when serum calcium is below the lower limit of normal.
Life-threatening hypocalcemia has been reported and can prolong QT, lower seizure threshold, worsen hypotension/heart failure, or cause arrhythmia.
teaching: Teach patients to report tingling, muscle spasms, severe cramping, fainting, or seizure activity.
delegationScope: Routine administration can be performed within medication scope; interpretation of calcium/PTH trends and symptomatic deterioration requires licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Giving cinacalcet despite a clearly low calcium because the PTH remains high.
oneLinePearl: Cinacalcet lowers PTH by convincing the body calcium is higher—so real calcium can fall.
sourceBasis: DailyMed cinacalcet U.S. prescribing information, current 2026

title: Calcitriol: Active Vitamin D, Active Calcium Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Calcitriol is active vitamin D used in selected CKD and hypoparathyroid states. Because it increases calcium and phosphate absorption, the safety problem is not 'vitamin toxicity' in the abstract—it is real hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia and ectopic calcification that require lab-guided therapy.
recognize: Hypercalcemia may cause nausea, constipation, weakness, polyuria, confusion or dysrhythmia.
High calcium plus high phosphate increases soft-tissue and vascular calcification risk, especially in kidney disease.
priorities: Review calcium, phosphorus, renal/dialysis context, other vitamin D products and calcium supplements.
Assess new weakness, confusion, GI symptoms or rhythm complaints when calcium rises.
Escalate significant hypercalcemia or symptomatic dysrhythmia.
assessMonitor: Trend serum calcium and phosphorus closely during titration, plus PTH and renal parameters according to indication.
interventions: Avoid adding non-prescribed vitamin D or calcium supplements without clinician review.
Coordinate phosphate-control therapy in CKD rather than treating calcitriol in isolation.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling warns that excessive calcitriol can cause hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria and hyperphosphatemia.
Patients on digitalis are at greater arrhythmia risk when hypercalcemia develops.
teaching: Teach patients not to self-add high-dose vitamin D or calcium and to keep ordered lab appointments.
delegationScope: Routine medication administration is within scope; interpretation of calcium/phosphate trends and toxicity requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Assuming calcitriol is harmless because it is a vitamin D product.
oneLinePearl: Calcitriol is active vitamin D—treat it like an active drug, not a supplement.
sourceBasis: DailyMed calcitriol U.S. prescribing information, current 2026

title: Patiromer: Potassium Binder, Not a Resuscitation Drug
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Patiromer binds potassium in the gastrointestinal tract for ongoing hyperkalemia management, but delayed onset means it must not replace emergency therapy for life-threatening hyperkalemia. It can also bind other oral medications and lower magnesium.
recognize: A patient with ECG changes, severe weakness, syncope or unstable hyperkalemia needs emergency stabilization rather than waiting for an oral binder to work.
Constipation and hypomagnesemia are clinically important adverse effects.
priorities: Check current potassium, magnesium, bowel function, medication schedule and whether the patient is clinically stable.
Separate other oral medications according to current labeling unless a drug is specifically exempted.
Escalate unstable hyperkalemia or significant hypomagnesemia.
assessMonitor: Trend potassium, magnesium, bowel pattern and effectiveness of the chronic hyperkalemia plan.
interventions: Prepare the powder as directed and never administer it dry.
Keep oral-medication timing organized to avoid clinically important binding interactions.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling states patiromer should not be used as emergency treatment for life-threatening hyperkalemia because of delayed onset.
Other oral medications generally require separation by at least 3 hours unless specifically shown not to have a clinically important interaction.
complications: Persistent hyperkalemia if used in place of emergency treatment
teaching: Teach that this is a maintenance potassium binder, not a rescue medication, and that medication timing matters.
delegationScope: Routine administration can occur within scope; unstable hyperkalemia requires immediate licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Giving patiromer as the only intervention to a patient with severe hyperkalemia and widening QRS complexes.
oneLinePearl: Patiromer lowers potassium slowly—an unstable heart cannot wait.

title: Sodium Zirconium Cyclosilicate: Bind Potassium, Count Sodium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate lowers potassium through GI binding but is not an emergency substitute for membrane stabilization or rapid intracellular shifting. Because it delivers sodium and can cause edema, fluid status matters in patients with heart or kidney disease.
recognize: Edema may worsen in patients already prone to fluid overload.
Severe constipation, bowel obstruction or major motility problems can make the drug inappropriate or ineffective.
priorities: Check potassium trend, volume status, edema, bowel function and concurrent oral medications.
Use emergency hyperkalemia treatment when the patient is unstable rather than relying on this binder.
Escalate worsening fluid overload or severe GI dysfunction.
assessMonitor: Trend potassium, weight, edema, BP, heart-failure symptoms and bowel function.
interventions: Prepare as an oral suspension exactly as directed.
Separate other oral medications according to the current product interaction instructions.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling states the drug should not be used as emergency treatment for life-threatening hyperkalemia due to delayed onset.
The current label warns about edema and notes substantial sodium content; other oral medications are generally separated by at least 2 hours.
complications: Persistent dangerous hyperkalemia if used as rescue therapy
GI complications in severe motility disorders
teaching: Teach patients to report swelling or rapid weight gain and to follow the medication-separation plan.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be performed within scope; unstable potassium or acute fluid overload requires licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Choosing a potassium binder as the immediate treatment for a patient with hyperkalemic ECG instability.
oneLinePearl: Bind potassium, but remember the sodium—and never confuse maintenance with rescue.
sourceBasis: DailyMed Lokelma (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) U.S. prescribing information revised 2026-03

title: Acetazolamide: Bicarbonate Loss Changes Acid-Base
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, increasing renal bicarbonate loss. That mechanism explains both its uses and its hazards: metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, volume effects and altered ventilation tolerance matter more than memorizing that it is simply a 'diuretic.'
recognize: Paresthesias, fatigue, tachypnea, confusion, worsening weakness or abnormal electrolytes can reflect acid-base/electrolyte effects.
Kidney dysfunction, impaired ventilation and diabetes increase risk from acid-base or electrolyte disturbance.
priorities: Review electrolytes, bicarbonate/acid-base context, renal function, respiratory status and concurrent high-dose aspirin use.
Monitor for worsening metabolic acidosis or significant potassium/sodium loss.
Escalate severe acidosis, neurologic change, serious sulfonamide-type reaction or major electrolyte abnormality.
assessMonitor: Trend bicarbonate/acid-base status when indicated, sodium, potassium, renal function, CBC/platelets for longer therapy, and symptoms of severe hypersensitivity.
interventions: Promote only the prescribed hydration/electrolyte plan; do not independently replace potassium without considering renal function and current levels.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling warns about metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia, hypokalemia and severe sulfonamide-related reactions.
High-dose aspirin with acetazolamide has been associated with severe toxicity including metabolic acidosis, coma and death.
teaching: Teach patients to report severe weakness, rapid breathing, confusion, rash, or unusual bleeding and to avoid unreviewed high-dose aspirin use.
delegationScope: Routine administration can occur within scope; interpretation of acid-base or severe electrolyte changes requires licensed assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Treating acetazolamide like an ordinary loop/thiazide diuretic and ignoring the bicarbonate loss and metabolic acidosis risk.
oneLinePearl: Acetazolamide dumps bicarbonate—follow the acid-base story, not just the urine output.
